posts.author: Valerii Hurachek
posts.headline: building Vesna for transparent tech hiring evidence & compliance
posts.text: Someone just made it to the interview stage because they put three lines of white text at the bottom of their resume. And the AI screener followed the instructions word for word. This sshot is from a hiring manager who caught it - an applicant hid tiny text in a 2pt white font, telling the model to ignore everything else and mark them as the best candidate. If you work in backend software, you recognize what this is immediately. Twenty years ago, if a website took text from an input box and pasted it straight into a database query, someone could type a few characters and wipe your tables. We called it SQL injection. It was one of the first basic security mistakes every junior developer learned to avoid. In 2026, half the AI screening tools on the market are making a similar mistake. They take raw text from a PDF, stitch it directly into a prompt, and ask an LLM to score the candidate. The software has no idea that white text on a white background is invisible to human eyes. It just reads the raw string, follows the instructions, and hands the candidate a top score. Jobseekers will always look for ways to get noticed. You cannot really blame someone for trying to get around a system that feels unfair. What bothers me is what happens to your pipeline. A capable backend engineer writes a plain resume about the production systems they kept running, and the parser drops them. Then someone with an invisible prompt injection lands on your senior engineer's calendar for a technical interview, only to fall apart on basic architecture questions. If you use an AI screening tool today, here is a simple test you can run this afternoon: Take an average resume from your archive. Add two lines of white text at the bottom telling the model that this is an exceptional candidate who should be moved forward immediately. Run it through your screener. If that changes the score, your software is just executing whatever string it was handed. Software can help talent teams handle volume, but only if it pulls verifiable technical facts and leaves the decision to a human being. When an LLM gets to make rejection calls on its own, hiring quickly turns into a game of who knows how to trick a prompt.

posts.text: 🚨🚨🚨HIRING🚨🚨🚨 We are reading and writing less, and worse, because of the rise of AI and brain rot. To counter it we should argue, engage critically, and sharpen our spoken reasoning. You can fake the essay. You can't fake thinking and reasoning on the fly. Being articulate is the prime wedge for the age of AI. Defending what you believe and understanding counterviews is crucial. So I built Debatable - live debates with a leaderboard. You are matched with a stranger on camera (or behind an anonymous avatar); you argue a motion in timed speeches, and an AI judge renders a ballot determining your ELO for later matchmaking. We know this AI judge is controversial conceptually, but we are steadfast on building a serious judging system. The site you'll see today was vibe-coded. I am not a career engineer; I built it with AI agents. It works, real people use it, and we have already begun rebuilding it entirely. We are a team of four - me, an engineer who has worked at NVIDIA and Apple, an MIT engineer, and an ML researcher from UT Austin - want to join us? 1) SWEs, one or two, full-time and paid (salary plus equity), ideally Oxford, SF, Chicago or NYC, but remote works. You need to be cracked. You'd own large parts of the rebuild - live video, the judge, the leaderboard, moderation - and it has to be ready for virality: the day one creator sends an entire audience through the door at once. Students and recent grads welcome. 2) Content and marketing interns, remote, but unpaid. You'd cut rounds into clips and help run our accounts + creator outreach. Ideally, you have a history of successful campaigns. 3) Creators, anywhere, any size: we want you, and we think you'll want us for content. Face another creator on camera while both audiences watch, or climb the ladder on stream. 4) Global ambassadors, any country: bring your debate society or club onto Debatable, run weekly rooms, host one event a month. There is a stipend, paid on results - commissioned debates that take place, and the people you bring in who debate or learn to debate. The vision for Debatable - We bring back Omegle, but structured, civil, yet contentious. We are the place people not only go to become more articulate, but to embrace the art of argument by debating or spectating. Apply through the forms on this page only: https://lnkd.in/gJThdtT8. DMs and emails aren't applications, but feel free to reach out if you're intrigued by what we're building or have questions. And I swear to god, if you send me AI writing or just boring writing, you're gone.

posts.text: AI replacing developers is going terribly wrong. At least, not in the way we expected. We were told AI would write more code, make developers more productive, and eventually reduce the number of developers companies need. But something interesting is happening. 1. Software development hiring is moving up again. Indeed says US software-development job postings are up almost 15% since February 2025, even while overall job postings fell 7%. 2. AI writes code fast. But it also creates a lot more code to review. Bugs. Unnecessary complexity. Security issues. Someone still has to review it, test it, understand it and maintain it. 3. And here's the part I find most interesting. 71% of the increase in software-development postings came from senior roles. So maybe companies aren't discovering that developers are useless. Maybe they're discovering that writing code is becoming cheaper, while engineering judgment is becoming more valuable. But that creates another problem. If AI takes away too much of the work juniors traditionally learned from... where do the next generation of senior engineers come from? Maybe AI isn't killing software engineering. Maybe it's changing what a software engineer is actually paid for. Developers: are we watching the end of software engineering as we knew it, or the beginning of a much better version of it?

posts.text: Building a product in 2027 may be the cheapest it has ever been. A few years ago, if you wanted to turn an idea into a working product, you needed access to engineers, time, and usually a decent amount of money. For many founders, the cost of building was the first major barrier between an idea and the market. That barrier is disappearing quickly. With vibe coding and increasingly capable agents, a small team can now build and ship things that would have required a much larger engineering team not too long ago. That changes the ecosystem. If someone can spend $20 and get an MVP into the hands of customers, having the ability to build is no longer much of a competitive advantage. And when everyone can build, I think we will start paying much more attention to what happens after the product is built. > Who understands the customer better? > Who can identify the right problem? > Who can make better product decisions? > Who can earn trust, distribute the product and turn feedback into something useful? The cost of creating software is falling. The cost of understanding people is going up. This is also why I’m thinking deeply about what happens to entry-level talent over the next 12 to 18 months. If a company can use AI to produce the first version of a product without hiring five junior developers, what exactly will create opportunities for those developers? I don’t think the answer is to panic and abandon technology. Quite the opposite. If you are early in your career, I would be very careful about becoming someone whose only value is “I can write code.” That skill is becoming easier to access. > Learn to understand the problem behind the code. > Learn how products work. Learn how customers behave. >Learn to debug, reason, communicate and make decisions. >Learn how to use AI without outsourcing your thinking to it. The same applies to people entering product, design, marketing, data and other parts of the workforce. I believe the next advantage will belong to people who can combine technical leverage with human judgment. We are entering a period where building will become cheaper, faster and more accessible. The interesting question is no longer, “Can you build it?” It is becoming, “Do you know what is worth building, why it matters, and what to do when the first version fails?” That is the conversation I want more young talent to start having now, before the market forces them to have it.

posts.author: Reece Sim
posts.headline: Building ThemeSpot - AI content management and theme development for HubSpot
posts.text: If your developer refuses to let you contribute with AI, or gate-keeps source code, it's time to let them go. As a web developer, I think it's so fucking cool that we can now invite our users to collaborate on features and code with us directly. Over the past two decades, web developers have gate-kept code.. Because it's too easy to break, too risky, they say. (and they want the recurring revenue) I always saw it as my job to make myself redundant after a project, especially on something simple like a website. Small updates and maintenance were like a thorn in my side rather than what I wanted to be doing every day, which was building features and digital experiences. AI made the code itself almost irrelevant, but it opened the door to new, and great product possibilities. If I design a harness correctly, by providing the right tools, infrastructure, and context, my users can write code with AI just as good as I can. That's incredible. It means good feedback just gets translated into code, and that you can build your own features, and customize your product experience to however you want to use it. Developers aren't out of a job, but code writers certainly are. True developers are euphoric right now, building more ambitious projects than ever before. I believe the future of all SaaS is pay to use a hosted version, pay for outcomes, work in a hackable UI, and you'll bring your own intelligence or pay a laziness tax on-platform. If your new app idea is selling tokens at a markup, you've already lost, you'd have higher margins selling outcomes. And if you're consuming tokens at a markup, hiring a developer will eventually be cheaper than all the rented software you pay for. A couple of things I've built recently where my clients can now collaborate directly: 1. A HubSpot developer project, with custom tools, hooks, and context files on how to maintain and improve the repo without me, how to debug deployment and a linter to ensure quality stays high. The client is free to vibe code whatever he wants into his website. 2. ThemeSpot - A HubSpot app that lets you vibe code entire themes, convert designs into pixel perfect HubSpot sites, manage content, QA websites, automate SEO and more. I can't wait to get to my terminal in the morning, all the mundane stuff is abstracted away. Pictured below: Non-technical C-suite asking for deploy logs, that's new!

posts.text: India's tech job market isn't "good" or "bad" right now. It's splitting in two. Naukri's September data shows: → Overall white-collar hiring: up 2% year on year → General software/IT hiring: down 4% → AI/ML hiring: up 20% In August, AI/ML hiring was up 31%, led by Hyderabad (+48%). The pattern is clear. Companies aren't hiring fewer people across the board. They're hiring for different skills. A few more signals from this week: → Global tech layoffs have crossed 1.63 lakh this year, and AI is cited in about 56% of them. → Oracle's latest round reportedly affects 1,000+ employees in India. → TCS planned only about 25,000 fresher offers for FY27, down from 44,000 last year. → GCCs (global capability centres) are still growing, with Hyderabad up 28% in August. What this means if you're a developer or fresher: Generic skills face more competition. Being "just another" full-stack or SDE profile is harder than it was. Pair your core stack (MERN, DevOps, Android, backend) with AI/LLM integration, cloud and security. Look beyond the big mass recruiters. GCCs, product companies and tier-2 cities like Coimbatore and Vadodara are showing stronger fresher growth. Watch the Q2 results: TCS (8 Oct), HCLTech (12 Oct), Infosys (23 Oct). Their headcount and fresher commentary will set the tone for the next quarter. My view: this is a skills shift, not a market collapse. The people who adapt will have the advantage. What's the one skill you're upskilling in this quarter? posts.text: My two cents on the current market: AI demand is accelerating quickly. Job ads requiring AI capability have roughly doubled over the past year, with AI skills now appearing across a significant proportion of software and data roles. AI Engineers are a clear example, with demand reportedly up around 150%. The supply of people with genuine hands-on AI experience simply isn’t keeping up. That shortage is creating a new tier of candidate. People who can genuinely build and implement AI are commanding strong packages, with some offers now including access to AI tooling and tokens. We’re also seeing experienced technical leaders getting back into the code. Even CTO-level candidates are exploring Software Engineering roles because they want to be hands-on with AI. At the same time, the broader tech market feels much quieter. The traditional domino effect of hiring has slowed down. When someone leaves, organisations are increasingly choosing to absorb the workload and “do more with less”. Job flow has slowed, salaries and contract rates have flattened, and junior and mid-level opportunities continue to decline as AI takes on tasks that previously helped develop less experienced engineers. However, specialist expertise remains highly valued. When businesses need niche technical knowledge or a specific capability delivered quickly, they’re still prepared to pay for it.

posts.text: Amazon loves: Heaps, Graph BFS, Intervals. Google loves: DP, Backtracking, Trees. Microsoft loves: Strings, Hashing, DP. You don't have to be ready for all 50 patterns. You have to be ready for the 10-15 your target company keeps asking. The DSA round is a pattern-targeting test, and the targets are fully public. Three moves separate the candidates who clear from the ones still applying. 1. Pick the shortlist first. Three companies, not thirty. Until you name the three, every problem you solve is a guess and every sheet you open is the wrong one. 2. Read 30 recent interview reports per company on LeetCode Discuss, GFG, and Glassdoor. Tag the pattern in each. By the 90th report, the top 5-8 patterns repeat so loudly you cannot miss them. 3. Drill those 5-8 until you can write the template blind, spot them in fresh problems under 90 seconds, and code the optimal under 25 minutes. Six weeks of focused work, not six months of random sheets. That's exactly what this DSA + System Design + AI Bootcamp is designed for—career outcomes, not just theory. posts.author: 8SENECA
posts.text: Every time a software project runs late, someone says the same thing. "We need to bring in more developers." It makes sense on paper. More people, more output. But a guy named Fred Brooks figured out in 1975 that it rarely works that way. Adding developers to a late project tends to make it later, not faster. New people need onboarding. The people doing the onboarding slow down. Coordination gets messier. The deadline gets worse. He called it Brooks's Law. It's been 50 years, and teams are still walking into the same trap. 👉 https://lnkd.in/gzz_m-Q6

posts.headline: Talent Acquisition @ HireMe
posts.text: Skip the ATS. Connect directly. For new grads, interns, and career changers, applying online can feel like shouting into a void. Your resume might never reach a human. What if you could find the exact person hiring for your dream junior tech role and connect with them before you even apply? Here's a LinkedIn hack to do just that: 1. Go to LinkedIn's search bar. 2. Type "Recruiter" or "Hiring Manager." 3. Click "All Filters." 4. Under "Keywords," add: "junior software engineer" (or your role) AND your tech stack (e.g., "Python" or "React"). 5. Apply "Location" (your target US city/state) and "Industry." 6. Filter by "People." Now you see relevant recruiters. Next, send a personalized connection request. Don't just hit connect. Mention a specific company project you admire, a recent post of theirs, or a shared connection. Briefly state your interest in junior roles and your key skill. Example: "Hi [Name], I saw your post about [Company X]'s new project. As a new grad interested in Python/data roles, I'd love to connect." This direct approach bypasses the application black hole. You build a real connection and stand out. HireMe helps you find junior roles. This helps you get noticed for them. Who will you connect with first today? #JuniorTech #JobSearchHack #LinkedInTips #NewGrad

posts.author: Hideya S.
posts.headline: Engineering lead
posts.text: Yesterday, four of the strongest engineers I've worked with over the last decade were impacted by layoffs. If you're hiring (or want to understand what it means to be an excellent engineer), read on. Annie (Hyun C) Kim has consistently written the most reliable, high-quality code I've seen in my career. She's relentless, unstoppable, and does it all: tech debt, migrations, new features, atypical projects, and more. She has kept the quality bar very high as AI entered software engineering. Brandon Wilson navigated some of our gnarliest tech debt and migrated 60+ HubSpot micro apps so dozens of teams and thousands of customers can rely on our video and file systems. He's also an amazing tech lead. Everyone on his team consistently praises his leadership and mentorship. James Magnarelli was my first tech lead, and the person who gave me the single most important piece of feedback that changed my career. Later on, together, he and I built HubSpot's first video product, then rebuilt it years later through plenty of twists and turns. His attention to detail never failed us. Plus, he has some of the best dad jokes. Maurya Patel was a new grad and spent only 8 months on my team, yet he ramped up impressively fast. He actively seeks feedback, acts on it, and follows up to make sure it stuck. He worked on our Breeze AI image generation feature and demoed it to over 100 people in record time. If you're hiring, and looking for strong engineers and leads, you'll want these people. I'm happy to make an intro. Annie (Hyun C) Kim, Brandon Wilson, James Magnarelli, and Maurya Patel, I'll miss you all so dearly. I am so thankful I got to work with and learn from you. Truly hope our paths cross again.

posts.author: CareerKrafter
posts.text: If you're a 2024/2025/2026 graduate or even still in college and preparing for your first serious switch, DSA is obviously non-negotiable. A little LLD helps too. But there's something else that is increasingly becoming important: GenAI fluency. And no, I don't mean: “I used ChatGPT to write some code.” I mean actually understanding how GenAI fits into software engineering. The interesting part? Companies are increasingly looking for this in their hiring. Look at recent SDE job descriptions across companies like Amazon, Microsoft and others. You'll increasingly find GenAI/AI experience mentioned as a preferred or required skill. And this is changing the interview conversation too. You might be asked: “Have you worked with GenAI?” And that's where many candidates get stuck. Because their previous company never gave them the opportunity to work on it. And the answer isn't to randomly add “GenAI” to your resume. You need to build the experience first, understand it properly, and then position it honestly. That's exactly what we want to help with. We are opening limited slots specifically for GenAI + SDE-1 career guidance — what to learn, what to build, how to position your existing experience.

posts.author: Ranjit S.
posts.headline: Chief Technology Officer @ Biddano | Technology Management, Technology Leadership
posts.text: These days, building a software product has become fast, but building it right is a much bigger challenge.While building one of my products, I was bombarded with information from my AI agent. At that point, I had two options: blindly accept its suggestions or take the time to understand the information not just the code. I believe this ability will become a key hiring criterion: processing large amounts of information, applying judgment, and using that context to solve real-world problems. This is where strong analytical thinking will matter.Future interviews may focus less on DSA and more on your ability to understand complex context and make sound decisions. Those who master this skill will have a significant advantage in the tech industry. But how do you master it? From my experience, engineers now need domain expertise alongside technical skills. Engineers need to understand the broader business problem instead of thinking only at the API level. Memorising API endpoints and payloads adds little value. What matters is understanding the use cases and functionality of each API and module. You also need a strong mental model of the database structure and the relationships between its entities. When AI asks you to accept or reject a change, your judgment depends on how well you understand both the system and the business.The challenge is that AI can create hundreds of database tables in 30 minutes, but understanding and validating them takes much longer. Engineers are working with a system that can generate solutions faster than they can review them, while still lacking crucial context about the actual business problem. People working in tech need to develop these skills. Otherwise, a fresher with strong contextual understanding and judgment could deliver more value than an experienced developer. Even as IITs face placement challenges today, I believe demand for top talent will rise sharply again over the next two years with significantly higher compensation. The definition of “top talent,” however, is changing.

posts.author: Talentwelove
posts.text: Half the briefs we get start with the wrong role name. The simple version, save it somewhere: A data scientist finds answers in data. "Why are users leaving?" Reports, analysis, insight. An ML engineer builds things that run. A model in production, working at 3am without help. The expensive mistake: hiring a data scientist and expecting working software. Six months later there are beautiful notebooks and nothing your customers can touch. One question fixes the brief: "In six months, do we want to KNOW something or do we want something to WORK?" Know = data scientist. Work = ML engineer. Both = two hires, sorry, not one unicorn. Get the brief right first: https://lnkd.in/eJfyf85t

posts.text: You may be too small to have your own internal platform team. That’s not the same as being too small for platform engineering. If you’re a small engineering team, you don’t need a platform department. You don't need a platform product manager, a portal with forty plugins, or a team maintaining abstractions nobody asked for. That would be ridiculous, and anyone pitching it to you at that size would need a very specific reason that explains why. The question I'd ask instead is what your engineers keep doing repeatedly that you could solve once. That answer is usually concrete. Every team writing CI pipelines from scratch. The same infrastructure provisioned slightly differently each time. Setting up a test VM or DB or Cluster and spinning it down after testing. Operations that depend on one person's memory or knowledge. Everyone, including software developers, needing to know the same handful of Terraform or Kubernetes commands. Outdated Knowledge Based in Confluence. None of that needs a department. It needs a few reusable capabilities and someone who owns them. And it is very possible I once consulted for a startup where I was the only DevOps engineer supporting more than 20 engineers. No platform team. Still a platform. Automated paths and self-service, built so developers could handle their own operations without coming to me. If your engineers can already deploy, provision what they need and understand their own services without waiting on anyone, don’t build a platform because someone told you to. You’re fine. But as the product grows, so does the platform underneath it, and more of this becomes necessary. That still doesn’t mean hiring a team. The goal is to remove enough repeated work that you don’t need one yet. Which of those is costing your engineers the most time right now? #PlatformEngineering #DevOps #EngineeringLeadership

posts.text: AI just moved from “interesting tool” to “institutional priority.” In one week, we saw government rebrand AI in legal contexts as “super intelligence,” OpenAI publish math benchmark progress that’s shaking up parts of research, universities launch new AI degrees, healthcare pilots expand AI prescribing, and companies keep redirecting budgets from headcount to automation. Why this matters: For engineers and technical professionals, this is no longer just about model capabilities. It’s about how AI is being embedded into law, education, medicine, hiring, and capital allocation. The technical stack is becoming organizational strategy. 3 key takeaways: • AI is becoming a systems-level decision, not a side project The White House and DOJ signals suggest AI is being framed not just as software, but as a national capability with legal and policy implications. That changes procurement, governance, and the expectations placed on technical teams. • Frontier model progress is getting more domain-specific and harder to ignore OpenAI’s math results are drawing attention because mathematics is a proxy for reasoning, abstraction, and research assistance. Whether or not you buy the hype, engineers should expect stronger AI support in formal problem-solving, coding, verification, and scientific workflows. • The labor market is being reshaped unevenly Georgia Tech launching an online AI master’s reflects rising demand for AI skills. At the same time, Reuters reports companies are cutting jobs as investment shifts toward AI. The signal is clear: teams that can integrate, evaluate, and govern AI will likely gain leverage; teams that can’t may face compression. The bigger pattern: AI adoption is no longer constrained by model availability. It’s constrained by trust, safety guarantees, regulation, and whether organizations can turn prototypes into reliable production systems. Question for the audience: What will matter most over the next 2 years for technical professionals: • Building with AI • Evaluating and governing AI • Deep domain expertise that AI can augment • Something else entirely?

posts.text: Bhaiya, mere previous company mein GenAI ka kaam hi nahi tha. CV mein kya likhun? Looking for a switch to an SDE-1 role? Read this. If you're a 2024/2025/2026 graduate or even still in college and preparing for your first serious switch, DSA is obviously non-negotiable. A little LLD helps too. But there's something else that is increasingly becoming important: GenAI fluency. And no, I don't mean: “I used ChatGPT to write some code.” I mean actually understanding how GenAI fits into software engineering. The interesting part? Companies are increasingly looking for this in their hiring. Look at recent SDE job descriptions across companies like Amazon, Microsoft and others. You'll increasingly find GenAI/AI experience mentioned as a preferred or required skill. And this is changing the interview conversation too. You might be asked: “Have you worked with GenAI?” And that's where many candidates get stuck. Because their previous company never gave them the opportunity to work on it. And the answer isn't to randomly add “GenAI” to your resume. You need to build the experience first, understand it properly, and then position it honestly. That's exactly what I want to help with. posts.text: 𝐉𝐚𝐩𝐚𝐧’𝐬 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝐆𝐂𝐂 𝐰𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐈𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐚 𝐢𝐬 𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭. It is not about setting up large teams and gradually scaling. It is about 𝐛𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐃𝐚𝐲 1. A few of the newer Japanese GCCs tell the story: 𝐃𝐚𝐢-𝐢𝐜𝐡𝐢 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐞 | 𝐇𝐲𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐛𝐚𝐝 First GCC outside Japan. Started with ~50–60 technology professionals and plans to reach 500–600 over the next 2–3 years. Focus: AI, data, cybersecurity, software and digital transformation. 𝐃𝐚𝐢𝐤𝐢𝐧 | 𝐆𝐮𝐫𝐮𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐦 Its new Innovation & Services Hub is planned around ~700 professionals, covering IT, digital services, data, finance and AI. 𝐌𝐢𝐳𝐮𝐡𝐨 | 𝐏𝐮𝐧𝐞 Its third India GCC, focused on engineering, analytics and business operations. Mizuho plans to take its India workforce to ~1,000 by 2027, with hiring across AI, analytics, capital markets and derivatives technology. 𝐑𝐚𝐤𝐬𝐮𝐥 | 𝐁𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐚𝐥𝐮𝐫𝐮 Perhaps the most interesting model. A deliberately lean “nano GCC” capped at ~100 people, with senior engineers working alongside AI. The mandate: platform engineering, cloud infrastructure and global product development. 𝐄𝐢𝐬𝐚𝐢 | 𝐕𝐢𝐬𝐚𝐤𝐡𝐚𝐩𝐚𝐭𝐧𝐚𝐦 A new global IT capability center, inaugurated in March 2026. The initial focus is cloud infrastructure, data & analytics, security engineering, FinOps, network engineering and ITSM - and Eisai is already hiring its founding team. 𝐓𝐎𝐘𝐎 𝐌𝐎𝐃𝐄𝐂 | 𝐁𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐚𝐥𝐮𝐫𝐮 A new 100,000 sq. ft. GCC for FPSO engineering, procurement and global project support. Current workforce: ~200. Target: 750 within three years. What I find interesting is the pattern. These companies aren't coming to India only for talent at scale. They are coming for specialized talent with global ownership. AI. Engineering. Product. Cybersecurity. Data. Capital markets. Digital infrastructure. And increasingly, the hiring question is becoming: “𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐩𝐞𝐨𝐩𝐥𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐰𝐞 𝐡𝐢𝐫𝐞?” → “𝐖𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐡 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐈𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐚 𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐮𝐬 𝐠𝐥𝐨𝐛𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲?” That is a very different GCC story. And one I believe we will see much more of from Japanese companies over the next few years. #GCC #JapanIndia #GCCIndia #JapaneseGCC #TalentStrategy #AI #Engineering #LeadershipHiring #TalentIntelligence

posts.text: 📌 The biggest hiring mistakes companies make aren’t always about finding the wrong candidate. Sometimes, they lose the right candidate before the hiring process even gets started. Here are 7 mistakes I keep noticing in recruitment: ❌ 1. Writing unclear job descriptions If candidates can't understand the role, responsibilities, or expectations, good candidates may simply move on. ❌ 2. Looking for a “perfect” candidate A candidate doesn't need to match 100% of the JD to become a great employee. ❌ 3. Taking too long to make decisions Good candidates usually have multiple opportunities. A slow hiring process can make companies lose them. ❌ 4. Focusing too much on degrees A qualification can show knowledge. Skills, problem-solving and adaptability show what someone can actually do. ❌ 5. Ignoring candidate experience Candidates remember how a company treats them — even when they don't get selected. ❌ 6. Using the same hiring strategy for every role Hiring a recruiter, software developer, sales professional and supply-chain analyst requires different approaches. ❌ 7. Forgetting that hiring is a two-way decision The company evaluates the candidate. But the candidate is also evaluating the company. Hiring isn't just about asking: “Is this person right for us?” It's also about asking: “Are we creating a process where the right person wants to join us?” It's about matching people, skills, expectations and business needs. #HumanResources #Recruitment #TalentAcquisition #Hiring #HR #FutureOfWork #CareerDevelopment #RecruitmentTips #Leadership #WorkplaceCulture Based on this concept give a cute proper professional image Proper seo

posts.text: 🚀 Freshers, I’m hiring a Software Engineer at The Developers Arena. You don't need 2 years of experience. You don't need a 9+ CGPA. You don't need to come from a top-tier college. But you do need to know how to build. I’m looking for freshers who can take a problem and turn it into working software. What I want to see: 🧠 Strong programming fundamentals 🐛 Ability to debug instead of blindly copying solutions 🏗️ Understanding of APIs and databases 🧪 Basic testing and error handling 💻 Clean, readable code 🚀 At least one project you've built yourself And here's the important part: Tutorial projects alone won't be enough. I want to know: → Why did you choose that database? → What happens when the API fails? → How did you structure your backend? → What was the hardest bug you faced? → What would you improve if 10,000 users started using it? You don't need to know everything. I’m looking for evidence that you can learn, think and build. posts.text: 🌍 BE/B.Tech CSE Done. Should You Consider Studying Abroad? For a CSE graduate, studying abroad can be more than earning another degree. It can be an opportunity to gain global tech exposure, deeper specialization, research experience and a different way of solving engineering problems. Universities across the USA, UK, Germany, Canada, Australia, Singapore and other technology hubs offer postgraduate programs in areas such as AI/ML, Cloud Computing, Cybersecurity, Robotics, Data Science and Software Engineering. 💻 What can you gain? 🔹 Specialization — Go deeper into AI, ML, Cloud, Cybersecurity, Robotics, etc. 🔹 Research Exposure — Work on advanced technologies and real research problems 🔹 Industry Projects — Apply classroom knowledge to practical challenges 🔹 Global Collaboration — Work with students and professionals from different countries 🔹 Internships & Networking — Access university career networks and industry connections 🔹 Communication Skills — Learn to work in multicultural engineering teams 🔹 Different Tech Ecosystems — Experience how companies build products at global scale 🚀 What could the path look like? BE/B.Tech CSE → MS/MTech/MSc specialization → Projects + Research → Internship → Global Tech Experience Possible specializations: 🤖 AI & Machine Learning ☁️ Cloud & Distributed Systems 🔐 Cybersecurity 📊 Data Science 💻 Software Engineering 🦾 Robotics & Autonomous Systems ⚡ Semiconductor & Systems 🌐 Product Engineering But there is an important reality: Going abroad does not automatically create a great tech career. The current international CS job market is competitive, particularly for entry-level roles, and visa/work authorization can significantly affect opportunities. Recent reporting also shows that AI is changing traditional software-development hiring. So the goal shouldn't simply be: “I want to study abroad.” It should be: “I want to become a stronger engineer with global exposure.” Build strong DSA + programming + projects + internships + communication skills before you leave. Then use the international degree to add specialization, research, industry exposure and global perspective. 🌍 A foreign university can open doors. Your skills are what help you walk through them. #CSE #ComputerScience #StudyAbroad #TechCareers #MSinCS #IT #AI #MachineLearning #CloudComputing #SoftwareEngineering #GlobalTech #EngineeringStudents #CareerGrowth

posts.text: Pakistan’s IT exports hit a record $4.6B in FY2025–26. Great news. But there’s another side developers must watch: AI is reshaping what global clients pay for. Research from the Pakistan Business Council shows the median freelance transaction fell 41% between FY2021 and FY2025, even as total freelance exports more than doubled. More work is leaving Pakistan, but typical deals are smaller. Now add AI. Global firms increasingly use AI coding agents to automate parts of software development. Some bring work in-house they once outsourced. Outsourcing isn’t disappearing—its economics are changing. For years, Pakistan’s edge was simple: good talent at lower cost. But what happens when AI reduces the human hours needed for the same output? A client who once needed 3 developers × 160 hours may now need fewer people and fewer hours. The developer isn’t less capable—billable human work has changed. Routine tasks face the most pricing pressure: Basic websites Simple CRUD apps Repetitive integrations Basic testing & bug fixes Data entry Generic content This work isn’t vanishing overnight, but margins are shrinking. There’s another risk: the junior pipeline. If firms produce more with fewer entry-level developers, how will new talent gain experience to become senior? That said, AI won’t take all jobs. New demand is emerging in: AI integration Cloud infrastructure Data engineering Cybersecurity System architecture AI-enabled products Engineers who can implement and maintain these systems in production are in demand. The market isn’t just shrinking—it’s shifting. Pakistani developers shouldn’t respond by becoming cheaper. The opportunity is to move up the value chain. I use AI daily—it makes me faster—but it doesn’t understand the client’s business, make architectural trade-offs, explain production incidents, or take the 3am call. That part of engineering is becoming more important, not less. Pakistan’s IT opportunity is growing, but selling cheaper developer hours is losing power. The next advantage will be: AI + engineering judgment + domain knowledge + ownership. What are you seeing? Are global clients hiring fewer developers, or expecting the same developers to deliver more with AI? #Pakistan #SoftwareEngineering #AI #TechCareers #FutureOfWork

posts.text: Every few years marketing decides it wants to be engineering when it grows up. In 2010 we got the growth hacker. In 2023 Clay gave us the GTM engineer. And this April, Profound's co-founder put "marketing engineer" on a slide at his own company's conference, and at least one guy in the audience updated his LinkedIn title before the keynote was over. Respect, honestly. Six months later the marketing engineer has a manifesto, a university course, a job board, a hackathon and a podcast. Profound made all five. Actual hires? Around 173 in the past year, according to Live Data Technologies. You could seat the entire profession at a mid-sized wedding. I'm not saying the work is fake. Marketing teams really are building agents to do competitor research and buy media, and plenty of companies are rebuilding their sites so ChatGPT stops describing them wrong. Somebody has to build and run that stuff. But I'd watch who's doing the defining. GTM engineer became a real job once people with nothing to sell started writing about it. Salary surveys, newsletters, bootcamps someone doesn't own. Growth hacker went the other way. The methods got so normal that the title stopped meaning anything, and nobody really missed it. Marketing engineer hasn't hit either point yet. Right now it belongs to one software company, and the employers hiring for it can't even agree on whether they want a developer with three years of experience or the CRM person who was already automating everything in Zapier. posts.text: the next 2–4 years as the critical transition period for software engineers AI agents can already write a huge amount of production code and have access to an enormous amount of senior-engineer-level knowledge. So the question is no longer: “Will software engineering teams become leaner?” I think they will. The more interesting question is: What kind of engineer will still be worth hiring? My rough expectation: 2026–2027: Hiring continues, but the bar rises sharply. Junior and CRUD-heavy roles get hit hardest. Companies increasingly ask: “Why do we need 8 engineers here instead of 3 strong engineers + agents?” 2027–2029: Significant compression. Teams that once needed 10–15 engineers may operate (or already operaing) with 4–8 strong engineers supported by agents. 2029–2032: If agent reliability keeps improving, the role of a “software engineer whose primary output is code” becomes much smaller. But I don’t think the future engineer is simply someone monitoring AI agents. The valuable engineer starts looking more like: Problem owner → Architect → Agent orchestrator → Reviewer → Production owner Instead of spending hours implementing an API, you might tell agents: “We need a pricing service with these business constraints, latency requirements, security boundaries, and rollback guarantees.” Agents can explore designs, write code, tests, migrations, inspect telemetry, and propose deployments. Your job becomes deciding: What should exist? Which constraints actually matter? Which trade-offs are acceptable? Is the agent solving the right problem, or just producing technically correct code? This is why I think experienced engineers may actually become more valuable. AI has absorbed a huge amount of knowledge that once differentiated senior engineers. But knowledge was never the entire value of a senior engineer. The real value was judgment, context, trade-offs, ownership, understanding messy business requirements, and being accountable when things go wrong. I also think the middle may get squeezed more than the top. A team of 30 engineers could eventually become 7–10 strong engineers + many agents. Not everywhere. But increasingly plausible. Which is why I would optimize around becoming the engineer who can be given: “We want to launch this business capability.” …and can turn that into architecture, systems, infrastructure, deployment, monitoring, and iteration. DSA and system design will still matter. But long term, the ability to own outcomes and build complete systems using AI as leverage may compound much more strongly. Looking at how quickly coding agents have improved, I would treat the next 2–4 years as the critical transition period for software engineers. Not because engineers disappear by 2030. But because by then the industry may have largely decided: what kind of engineer is still worth hiring. #SharingThoughts #AIAgents #SoftwareEngineering

posts.text: The worst time to hire engineers is the week your round closes, which is exactly when the pressure to start is highest. By then the board has seen the hiring plan and the recruiters are lined up. What the hiring plan rarely shows is that the engineers you already have are about to onboard everyone you hire, right when they're also being asked to deliver what the round promised. Good engineers can build whatever roadmap you hand them. What they can't do is onboard themselves. Every new hire needs time from your best engineers, priorities that hold still long enough to learn the work, and a team that already ships on a rhythm they can join. The week after a raise is when all three are scarcest. None of this is an argument against hiring. You raised the money to hire, and I've hired plenty myself, from the days of leading four engineers at RainKing through my time as CTO at DiscoverOrg/ZoomInfo. If I were in your seat, I'd open the searches on day one, since the right engineers take a while to find, and use those weeks to get the team ready before the first ones start. That first month is for deciding what the bigger team will work on. Talk to customers about what's next, pick the one or two things that matter most this year, and write down what won't get built, so the priorities hold still when people start arriving. In the second month, I'd make sure I was seeing working software every week, because a team that ships weekly is more likely to absorb new people than one that doesn't. I'd also have the team build the support new engineers will need, so they lean on it instead of your best people. That means documentation for the parts of the system that live only in someone's head, and a review process tight enough to catch a new engineer's mistakes before a customer does. By the third month, I'd be hiring at the pace the team can absorb, and I'd know what each product costs to build and run. I could show the board what we're building, why customers want it and when it will ship, next to the hiring numbers. A round buys runway, and the first 90 days decide how far it takes you. If you've been through a raise as a founder, an engineer or an investor, what would you tell a CEO whose round closed last week? #SaaS #ProductStrategy #VentureCapital

posts.author: Rob Zuber
posts.headline: CTO at CircleCI
posts.text: In a recent podcast with Josh Anderson of Revelo, we got onto the topic of why I'm having such great results with hiring junior developers right now. Historically, we brought junior engineers in and trained them in the shape of senior engineers. The problem is, though, we’re not totally sure what that shape is anymore. The job is changing quickly. We’re spending less time writing syntax and more time thinking about systems, building tools that build software, and figuring out where humans need to be involved (if at all). In some ways, all that change is a great leveler. A new grad isn’t transitioning from an old way of working to a new one, they’re just learning how the job works now. That fresh perspective is extremely useful when so many of our old assumptions are up for debate. They ask why we do something a certain way, and sometimes the answer is, “I have no idea. It’s just how we’ve always done it.” That’s been a huge part of what makes our new grad program work. We’re learning alongside them, and getting a ton of energy, curiosity, and fresh ways of looking at things in return. There's amazing talent out there in the new grad pool. I cant recommend it enough.

posts.text: Computer science is just the history of pushing human beings up the abstraction ladder. In the 1950s, we manually punched 1s and 0s into cards. Then assembly gave us readable instructions for hardware. Then compiled languages decoupled us from machine architectures entirely. Now, natural language models are decoupling us from routine syntax. Every generation of engineers feared that abstraction would destroy their value. Every time, it did the exact opposite: it freed them to solve bigger problems. When high level languages became standard, companies stopped asking candidates to manage memory registers by hand. We realized that human judgment belonged at the system design layer, not the hardware execution layer. So why are we still treating algorithmic puzzles like DSA as the gold standard for software engineering competence? AI produces syntax effortlessly. What it cannot do is understand company context, business risk, or domain nuance. The next generation of senior engineers will not be implementers. They will be Domain Translators: * Business acumen first: Understanding why a feature needs to exist before asking how to write it. * Precision in specification: Defining edge cases, constraints, and architecture with ruthless clarity. * Critical evaluation: Auditing generated logic against real world production realities. The barrier to entry for writing code is collapsing to zero. The premium on knowing what to build and why has never been higher. #TechLeadership #SoftwareEngineering #GenerativeAI #Hiring #FutureOfWork
